newsitem.title: USA: Power struggle looms at NRA meeting in Seattle.
newsitem.headline: Power struggle looms at NRA meeting in Seattle.

text.p: The National Rifle Association opens its 126th annual meeting on Friday against the backdrop of a fierce internal struggle that could reverberate far beyond the powerful gun-rights lobbying group.

A three-day exhibit of guns and gear with seminars on topics such as "Developing tomorrow's shooters today" will be only the warmup to the main event on Monday, when the group's 75-member board of directors meets to elect officers.

Executive vice president Wayne LaPierre, who runs the NRA's day-to-day operations, is expected to be re-elected but not without a fierce battle from hardliner Neal Knox, a former ally and the group's first vice president.

"I think it's looking good," LaPierre said in an interview. "The members are weighing in and they're solidly in our corner. They want to keep the association growing, they want to keep it in the mainstream."
But even if LaPierre keeps the post he has held since 1991, one of Washington's most powerful lobbies already has lost some of the clout it once had and could be damaged by the internecine struggle.
"They've lost a lot of ground over the years," said Mike Beard, president of the Coalition to Stop Handgun Violence. "But their demise has been predicted several times, and it's never happened yet."

Some 25,000 of the NRA's 2.8 million members are expected to pass through the Seattle convention centre during the three-day meeting, where Idaho Republican Sen. Larry Craig will be among the speakers.
The NRA's membership is down from a peak of 3.5 million, although LaPierre said it has risen from as low as 2.3 million in 1991, when he inherited the group with a $10 million budget deficit.
LaPierre said the group has operated in the black the past three years and has cash and other assets of $50 million, up from $41 million three years ago.
He brushes off rumours that the organisation is in financial trouble, pointing to a recent independent audit by the accountants Coopers & Lybrand.

"You had a small group of people that were trying to take over, and they put out a lot of false information about the financial condition of the organisation to try to propel their effort," he said. "It's been really destructive to the cause."
The battle between LaPierre and Knox appears to be one that pits a smooth Washington insider against a more rough-edged, take-no-prisoners approach.

"We would really like to see Neal Knox win," said Beard of the gun-control group. "He's much more obstreperous. ... That attitude that they've had in the past has helped alienate Congress, and we'd like to see them continue that."
Knox could not be reached for comment.

While a victory by Knox appears unlikely, according to observers within and outside the NRA, the battle could be politically damaging particularly to Republicans in Congress who benefit from the group's political largesse.

"Any time you have a vacuum at the top, the other side -- the gun control movement and President Clinton -- will try to step in and seize the moment," Georgia Representative Bob Barr told The American Spectator.
Since President Clinton's re-election last year, the NRA has scaled back its ambitions at least at the federal level, and no longer talks about repealing the ban on assault rifles as it once did.
But the group has been waging a state-by-state campaign aimed at expanding the right to carry a concealed weapon, now legal in 31 states.

In addition, a decision is expected from the Supreme Court soon in a lawsuit supported by the NRA that could weaken the federal Brady Bill requiring handgun registration. And the NRA this year was certified as a non-governmental organisation in the United Nations, where some member countries would like to see international handgun restrictions.
